guide:
# Atech SDK — guide for coding agents

You are helping someone make an **Atech board** do something. The board is an
ESP32-S3 with numbered ports; modules (button, light grid, sensors, motors, a robot
arm…) slide into the ports. You write one small file, `project.yaml`. The SDK turns
it into firmware, compiles it, flashes it, and then lets you talk to the board from
the laptop.

This text ships inside the package: `atech guide` prints it, and `atech new` puts a
copy in every project as `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`.

## The whole workflow

```bash
atech list-boards                  # ask the user which board they are holding
atech list-modules                 # what exists. Never invent a module
atech info <module>                # its C++ API, events, actions and cautions
atech new <name> --board 14port    # project.yaml + this guide
#   ...edit project.yaml...
atech describe <dir>               # what you placed, the API, the events and actions
atech validate <dir>               # placement check
atech build <dir>                  # generate + compile
atech upload <dir>                 # flash the board on USB
atech check                        # reboot it: which modules answered, and why not
atech monitor                      # events coming from the board
atech send <key> [value]           # one action, confirmed by the board (value: r=255 g=0, a number, or JSON)
```

Every command exits non-zero when it fails and says why on stderr (`error: …`, or
the list of placement issues). Cautions are printed on stdout with the result.
`list-boards`, `list-modules`, `info` and `monitor` take `--json`.

## project.yaml

```yaml
name: my_project
board: 14port                        # 8port | 10port | 14port
modules:
  - {id: button,   instance: btn, port: 1}
  - {id: neopixel, instance: led, port: 2}
  - {id: speaker,  instance: spk, ports: [13, 14]}   # 2-port module: an adjacent pair
code:
  setup: |
    // optional, runs once after every module is initialised
  loop: |
    // runs forever
    if (btn.wasPressed()) {
      led.setAll(255, 0, 0);
      led.show();
    }
```

- `instance` is the name of the C++ object you call in `code:`. Its methods are in
  `atech info <module>` and `atech describe`.
- Ports: `atech list-boards` shows which ports take modules and which of them have
  UART. A 2-port module needs two neighbouring ports; a UART module (the robot arm)
  needs a UART port. `atech validate` says what is wrong and which ports would work.
- **Ask the user which port each module is in.** You cannot see the board.
- Power modules (USB-C, power jack) are not in the catalog and need no entry in
  `project.yaml`: they carry no firmware. Leave the ports they sit in unused.
- There are exactly two code blocks, `setup` and `loop`. Keep state in `static`
  variables inside `loop`.
- `atech validate` checks placement only. Mistakes in your C++ show up in `atech build`.

## Rules for the `code:` block

- **Never block.** Use `millis()` for timing; no `delay()` beyond a few ms.
- **Edge calls are yours.** `btn.wasPressed()`, `knob.wasRotatedCW()`,
  `pir.wasTriggered()`, `imu.wasShaken()` return true once per edge and then clear.
  The firmware's own events to the laptop do not use them, so your code and the
  laptop both see every press. Call each edge function in one place only.
- **Do not read `Serial` yourself.** The generated firmware reads it to receive
  actions from the laptop. Reading it in your code steals those bytes.
- **Do not hardcode GPIO numbers.** Pins come from the port.
- **Do not edit `build/`.** It is regenerated on every `atech build`.
- To send your own event to the laptop, print one JSON line:

  ```cpp
  Serial.printf("{\"type\":\"event\",\"payload\":{\"event_type\":\"sensor\",\"key\":\"level\",\"value\":%d}}\n", level);
  ```

- To accept your own action from the laptop, test `atech_action` and confirm it:

  ```cpp
  if (atech_action == "buzz") { spk.playTone(880, 100); atechDone(); }
  ```

  `atech_value` holds the value as a `String`. An action nobody handles is
  answered with `ok:false`, so the laptop knows.

## Talking to the board from the laptop

`atech describe` lists the exact event and action names of a project. They are
built from the instance name, for example `btn`, `th_temperature`, `led_fill`.

```bash
atech monitor --key btn                          # only the button's events
atech send led_fill r=255 g=0 b=0                # prints ok only if the board did it
```

```python
from atech import Board, ActionRejected, NoAcknowledgement, NoBoardFoundError

with Board.connect() as board:                   # or Board.connect(port="/dev/cu.usbmodem1101")
    board.call("led_fill", {"r": 255, "g": 0, "b": 0})         # do something
    joints = board.query("arm_read", reply="arm_positions")   # ask, get the answer back
    last = board.latest("btn")                   # last event seen for a key, or None
    for event in board.events(keys=["btn"]):     # blocks, yields events forever
        print(event.key, event.value)
```

- `board.call(key, value="", timeout=2.0)` returns once the board confirmed. It
  raises `ActionRejected` when the board could not do it (no such action, bad value,
  a servo that does not answer) and `NoAcknowledgement` when nothing came back.
- `board.query(key, value="", reply=<event key>)` is `call` plus the value of the
  event the board answers with. Use it for every read-back.
- `board.send()` only writes to the port and tells you nothing. Use `call`.
- `Board.connect()` takes the first board on USB and raises `NoBoardFoundError` when
  there is none. With several boards attached, pass `port=` (`atech ports` lists them).
- Wait for each action before sending the next: a flood of unconfirmed ones can
  overflow the board's buffer and some get lost.
- **One program per board at a time.** A second program opening the same port gets
  `PortUnavailableError`. Stop `atech monitor` before `atech send` or `atech upload`,
  or listen and send from one Python script as above.

## Things that are true and save time

- **The first build downloads the ESP32 compiler** (about 2.4 GB on disk, once).
  After that a build takes seconds. Do the first build on good wifi. A few modules
  (the light grid, for one) also download a small library the first time a project
  uses them, so a new project can still need the network once.
- **`atech upload` always regenerates and rebuilds from `project.yaml`.** There is no
  stale build to worry about.
- **Port in use?** Only one program can hold the board's port. Close the other one
  (`atech monitor` in another terminal, an editor's serial monitor), or `atech free-port`.
- **Linux, "no permission":** `sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER`, then log in again.
- **No board found?** It must be plugged in with a USB data cable. `atech ports`
  shows what the SDK sees. The SDK never falls back to some other serial port.
- **`atech check` cannot see output-only modules.** A light grid or a display
  reports "initialized" even when nothing is plugged in. Only eyes confirm output.
- **A module does nothing?** Do not re-flash the same firmware. Print a line
  before and after the suspect call and watch `atech monitor --json`; swap the
  module into another port; keep one known-good module in the same build.
- **Displays:** `display()` redraws the whole screen and takes about 273 ms. Draw
  the background once, then use `displayRegion(x, y, w, h)` for what changes.

### Robot arm: power

The Robot Arm module passes the board's high-voltage rail (labelled 12 V) straight
to the servos. That rail is fed by a power module (the power jack module, or the
USB-C PD power module) and carries whatever that module is given. Nothing regulates
it, and the standard USB-C module does not feed it. SO-101 arms come in a 12 V and
a 5 V version, and a 12 V supply on a 5 V arm damages the servos.

Building is harmless. Before you **flash, or tell the user to connect or power the
arm**, ask which arm they have and what voltage is printed on the supply in the
jack, and tell them: 12 V supply for a 12 V arm, 5 V supply for a 5 V arm, never
more than 12 V. `atech validate`, `build` and `upload` print this as a `CAUTION`;
relay it. With nothing in the power jack the servos have no power, so a silent arm
on USB-C alone is expected.

The arm goes stiff when the firmware starts (torque is switched on in setup) and
moves as soon as something tells it to. Have the user clear its reach first.

### Robot arm: no servo answers

If the arm has power and `atech check` still reports it not responding: on a
Robot Arm V1.0 module with six servos, the servos only answered when the board
transmitted on the port's line B. The module transmits on line A by default. Swap
the two lines in `project.yaml` and upload again:

```yaml
  - {id: robot_arm, instance: arm, port: 3, swap_lines: true}
```

Tell the user which of the two worked.

## A module the catalog does not have

```
my_project/
├── project.yaml          # add:  modules_path: ./my_modules
└── my_modules/
    └── <id>/
        ├── module.yaml   # same shape as a bundled one
        ├── <id>.h
        └── <id>.cpp
```

Start from a bundled module: `python -c "import atech.catalog, pathlib;
print(pathlib.Path(atech.catalog.__file__).parent / 'data' / 'modules')"` prints
where they live. A module with the same id as a bundled one replaces it. In
`module.yaml`, every event you declare must be a key the `loop` template really
prints, and every action needs a `handler:` (C++ run when the action arrives;
the value is the `String value`).

## Never

- Invent a module, a method, an event or an action. `atech info` is the truth.
- Skip `atech validate`.
- Tell the user something worked because a command exited 0. Flashing succeeding
  says nothing about the hardware; check with `atech check`, `atech monitor`, or
  ask them what they see.
- Use `delay(1000)` in `loop`.
- Connect or power a robot arm before the supply question above is answered.

aht20.description:
AHT20 integrated temperature + humidity sensor over I2C (address 0x38).
Range -40 to +125 °C and 0-100 %RH. A background FreeRTOS task takes
measurements (~75 ms each) and caches them, so the getters return instantly
and never block your loop. Single port: SDA on Line A, SCL on Line B.

events.description: Temperature in degrees Celsius. Emitted every 2 s (cached reading).
Relative humidity in %RH. Emitted every 2 s (cached reading).

aht20.name: AHT20 Temperature & Humidity Sensor

button.description:
Single digital button input with edge detection. Active-low with internal
pull-up. Emits a sensor event with value 1 on press and 0 on release.

events.description: 1 on press edge, 0 on release edge

button.name: Button

actions.description: Set motor speed in [-255, 255]; negative = reverse.

dc_motor.description:
H-bridge DC motor driver. Two GPIO lines drive a small DC motor with PWM
speed and direction control. Accepts a single 'speed' action with value
in -255..255 (negative reverses direction).
dc_motor.name: DC Motor

distance_sensor.description:
ST VL53L5CX multi-zone Time-of-Flight distance sensor. Ranges an 8x8 grid
(64 zones) up to ~4000 mm. A background FreeRTOS task ranges at 15 Hz and
caches the grid, so the getters return instantly and never block your loop.
Single port: SDA on Line A, SCL on Line B. Uses the SparkFun VL53L5CX
library, which talks to Arduino `Wire` directly — the generated setup()
initializes the bus, the driver only shares it.

events.description: Closest object across all 64 zones, in mm. Returns the sentinel 32767 when nothing is in range (not 0 or -1). Emitted every 500 ms.

distance_sensor.name: Distance Sensor (VL53L5CX 8x8 ToF)

icm40608.description:
6-axis inertial measurement unit: 3-axis accelerometer (±2g), 3-axis
gyroscope (±250°/s), and on-die temperature. The driver auto-detects which
chip is present at boot (ICM-40608 at 0x68 or LSM6DSOX at 0x6A) — your code
is identical either way. A background FreeRTOS task polls at 100 Hz and
caches readings, so every getter returns instantly. Single port: SDA on
Line A, SCL on Line B.

events.description: Emitted once (value 1) on each shake/tap spike (>1.8 g by default).
Total tilt from upright (0 = flat face-up, 180 = face-down). Emitted every 1 s.
Coarse 6-way pose: face_up / face_down / edge_right / edge_left / edge_front / edge_back / unknown. Emitted every 1 s.

icm40608.name: 6-Axis IMU (ICM-40608 / LSM6DSOX)

microphone.description:
I2S MEMS microphone (ICS-43434) for sound-level detection and audio capture.
24-bit samples at 16 kHz. Spans TWO adjacent ports — placement requires an
adjacent pair like [1, 2] / [3, 4]. A background FreeRTOS task reads the I2S
bus (on I2S_NUM_1, so it won't clash with the speaker on I2S_NUM_0) and caches
the RMS/peak level, so the getters return instantly. Line A1 = LR select,
Line B1 = WS, Line A2 = SCK, Line B2 = SD.

events.description: Current RMS sound level, 0-32767. Emitted every 250 ms.

microphone.name: I2S MEMS Microphone (ICS-43434)

actions.description: Object {"r": 0-255, "g": 0-255, "b": 0-255} sets every LED to that colour.

neopixel.description:
3x3 grid of WS2812B / SK6812 LEDs. Drives both Line A (RGB) and Line B
(RGBW) so the same driver works for both module revisions. Accepts a
'pixel' action ({index, r, g, b}) and a 'fill' action ({r, g, b}).
neopixel.name: NeoPixel 3x3 Grid
neopixel.usage:
// Public API of NeoPixelGrid — the instance is `{{ instance }}`.
// 3x3 grid (9 LEDs). Always call show() after staging colors.
// Indices 0-8, or row/col 0-2. Brightness is clamped to 20% (51/255).
{{ instance }}.setAll(255, 0, 0);                   // every LED red
{{ instance }}.setPixel(4, 0, 255, 0);              // centre LED green
{{ instance }}.setPixelXY(0, 2, 0, 0, 255);         // top-right blue
{{ instance }}.setRow(1, 80, 80, 80);               // middle row dim white
{{ instance }}.setColumn(0, 0, 0, 0);               // left column off
{{ instance }}.clear();                             // stage all-off
{{ instance }}.show();                              // push to LEDs (do this!)
{{ instance }}.setBrightness(30);                   // 0..51 effective

pir.description:
AM312 mini passive-infrared motion sensor. A single digital OUT line goes
HIGH for ~2 s when motion is seen within its ~3-5 m / 100° cone, then
returns LOW. Hardware-debounced — no pull-ups needed. Uses only Line A.
The sensor needs ~30 s after power-on to thermally stabilise; isWarmedUp()
reports when readings can be trusted.

events.description: 1 on motion start (rising edge), 0 when motion clears (~2 s later). Suppressed during the 30 s warmup.

pir.name: PIR Motion Sensor (AM312)

actions.description: Move one joint: {"id":1-6,"position":0-4095,"timeMs":ms}. timeMs is optional (0 = as fast as the servo goes). Fails if the servo does not answer.

Move all 6 joints: {"positions":[p1..p6],"timeMs":ms} (0-4095 each). timeMs is optional (0 = as fast as the servos go). The move is broadcast: an ok means it was sent, not that the arm got there. Check with {{ instance }}_read.
Center all joints to 2048 over the given time in ms (1000 if no value is given).
Enable (true) or disable (false) holding torque on all joints.
Load a saved recording from flash slot 0-9 and play it back.
Read all 6 joints. Answers with the event {{ instance }}_positions = [p1..p6] (0-4095 each, -1 for a joint that did not answer), sent before the acknowledgement. Fails if no joint answers.

robot_arm.caution:
The Robot Arm module passes the board's high-voltage rail (labelled 12 V) straight to
the servos. That rail is fed by a power module (the power jack module, or the USB-C PD power
module) and carries whatever that module is given: nothing regulates it, and the
standard USB-C module does not feed it. So the supply
must match the arm. SO-101 arms come in a 12 V and a 5 V version: use a 12 V supply
for the 12 V arm and a 5 V supply for the 5 V arm. A 12 V supply on a 5 V arm damages
the servos. Never plug more than 12 V into the jack. Check the voltage printed on the
supply and which arm you have before you connect anything.
robot_arm.description:
6-axis robot-arm controller for the SO-101 / SO-ARM100 (Feetech STS3215 servos).
Needs a UART port.
Single port using half-duplex UART at 1 Mbps to drive 6 daisy-chained servos
(IDs 1-6, position 0-4095, center 2048, ≈0-240°). Supports per-joint and
synchronized moves, position/temperature read-back, motion recording &
playback, and 10 flash save-slots. TX on Line A, RX on Line B. **The module
passes the board's high-voltage rail to the servos: the arm gets whatever supply
is plugged into the power jack module (or comes from the USB-C PD power module), unregulated. The supply must match the arm
(12 V or 5 V). See `caution`.**

events.description: All 6 joint positions [p1..p6] (-1 = that joint did not answer), sent in answer to the {{ instance }}_read action.

robot_arm.name: SO-101 / SO-ARM100 6-Axis Robot Arm

rotary_encoder.description:
18-step quadrature rotary encoder with a push-button switch and a 12-LED
NeoPixel indicator ring. Spans TWO adjacent ports — placement requires an
adjacent pair like [1, 2] or [3, 4] on the 8-port board. Uses interrupts
for missed-step-free decoding at any speed, plus a background FreeRTOS
task that renders the ring indicator in ~1ms regardless of loop timing.

events.description: Cumulative knob position (acceleration applied). Emitted on every detent of rotation.
Emitted with value=1 each time the knob's push-button is pressed.

rotary_encoder.name: Rotary Encoder Knob

scd40_air_quality.description:
Sensirion SCD40 NDIR CO2 sensor over I2C (address 0x62) — true CO2
measurement (400-2000 ppm typical), with temperature and humidity returned
as calibration byproducts. A background FreeRTOS task polls the sensor at
its native 5 s cadence and caches the reading, so the getters return
instantly and never block your loop. The first valid reading lands ~5 s
after boot. Single port: SDA on Line A, SCL on Line B.

events.description: CO2 concentration in ppm. Reads 0 until the first measurement lands (~5 s after boot). Emitted every 5 s (cached reading).
Temperature in degrees Celsius. Emitted every 5 s (cached reading).
Relative humidity in %RH. Emitted every 5 s (cached reading).

scd40_air_quality.name: SCD40 Air Quality Sensor (CO2)

actions.description: RTTTL melody string, e.g. "tune:d=4,o=5,b=140:c,e,g,2c6". Plays in the background.

Base64-encoded 16-bit mono PCM at 16 kHz, at most ~3000 base64 characters per action (lines are capped at 4096). The host decodes an MP3/WAV, resamples to 16 kHz mono, and sends chunks. Blocks until the chunk has played.

speaker.description:
3W Class-D I2S audio amplifier (MAX98357A) for tones, chords, and full
melodies. Spans TWO adjacent ports — placement requires an adjacent pair
like [1, 2] / [3, 4] (8-port) or [1, 2] … [13, 14] (14-port). Audio plays
in a background FreeRTOS task on Core 0, so the main loop never blocks. The
RTTTL parser lets you play ringtone-style melody strings with a single call.
speaker.name: I2S Speaker (MAX98357A)

st7735_tft.description:
160x80 pixel colour TFT (ST7735 controller, SPI). Spans TWO adjacent ports.
65K colours (RGB565), text, shapes, and a flicker-free canvas buffer. Two
drawing modes: canvas mode (default — clear/draw/display, best for
dashboards) and direct mode (setDirectMode(true), best for games/animation).
Pin map: DC on Line A1, CS on Line B1, MOSI on Line A2, SCLK on Line B2.
st7735_tft.name: ST7735 TFT Color Display (160x80)

stepper_motor.description:
Bipolar stepper motor (e.g. NEMA 17) driven by a TMC2209 in STEP/DIR mode.
Spans TWO adjacent ports: STEP on Line A and DIR on Line B of the primary
port, ENABLE on Line A of the secondary port. Requires an EXTERNAL motor
supply (typically 12-24 V) wired to the driver board — the SDK can't detect
a missing VMOT, the symptom is "calls succeed but the motor doesn't move".
All motion calls are BLOCKING (they return once the pulses are issued).
stepper_motor.name: Stepper Motor Driver (NEMA 17 / TMC2209)
